title: Agreement & Tolerance Limits
text: replicates, x y need measured number times, within-subject variances estimated separately (Zou 2011). Compute subject means within-subject variances subject \(\) (\(= 1, \dots, n\)), \(m_{xi}\) measurements x \(m_{yi}\) measurements y: \[ \bar d_i = \bar x_i - \bar y_i, \qquad \bar d = \frac{1}{n} \Sigma_{=1}^{n} \bar d_i \] \(s_{xi}^2\) \(s_{yi}^2\) sample variances replicates x y within subject \(\). Compute pooled estimates within-subject variances \[ s_{xw}^2 = \Sigma_{=1}^{n} \frac{m_{xi}-1}{N_x-n} \cdot s_{xi}^2, \qquad s_{yw}^2 = \Sigma_{=1}^{n} \frac{m_{yi}-1}{N_y-n} \cdot s_{yi}^2 \] \(N_x = \Sigma_i m_{xi}\) \(N_y = \Sigma_i m_{yi}\). Compute variance subject mean differences (-subject variance) \[ s^2_b = \Sigma_{=1}^n \frac{ (\bar d_i - \bar d)^2}{n-1} \] Compute harmonic means replicate sizes \[ m_{xh} = \frac{n}{\Sigma_{=1}^n m_{xi}^{-1}}, \qquad m_{yh} = \frac{n}{\Sigma_{=1}^n m_{yi}^{-1}} \] Compute variance single difference \[ s_d^2 = s^2_b + \left(1 - \frac{1}{m_{xh}}\right) s_{xw}^2 + \left(1 - \frac{1}{m_{yh}}\right) s_{yw}^2 \] Calculate LME MOVER Method \[ u_1 = \left[s_b^2 \left(\frac{n-1}{\chi^2_{\alpha, n-1}} - 1\right)\right]^2 \] \[ u_2 = \left[\left(1-\frac{1}{m_{xh}}\right) s_{xw}^2 \left(\frac{N_x-n}{\chi^2_{\alpha, N_x-n}} - 1\right)\right]^2 \] \[ u_3 = \left[\left(1-\frac{1}{m_{yh}}\right) s_{yw}^2 \left(\frac{N_y-n}{\chi^2_{\alpha, N_y-n}} - 1\right)\right]^2 \] \[ u = s_d^2 + \sqrt{u_1 + u_2 + u_3} \] \[ LME = \sqrt{\frac{z_{1-\alpha}^2 \cdot s_b^2}{n} + z_A^2 \cdot \left(\sqrt{u}-\sqrt{s^2_d}\right)^2} \] Bland-Altman Method \[ S_{LoA}^2 = \frac{s^2_b}{n} + \frac{z_A^2}{2 \cdot s_d^2} \cdot \left(\frac{s_b^4}{n-1} + \left(1-\frac{1}{m_{xh}}\right)^2 \frac{s_{xw}^4}{N_x - n} + \left(1-\frac{1}{m_{yh}}\right)^2 \frac{s_{yw}^4}{N_y - n}\right) \] \[ LME = z_{1-\alpha} \cdot S_{LoA} \] Calculate LoA \[ LoA_{lower} = \bar d - z_A \cdot s_d \] \[ LoA_{upper} = \bar d + z_A \cdot s_d \] Calculate LoA CI \[ Lower \space CI = LoA_{lower} - LME \] \[ Upper \space CI = LoA_{upper} + LME \]

title: Agreement Tests
text: Step 1: Calculate Individual Subject Means Variances \[ \bar x_i = \frac{1}{n_{xi}} \Sigma_{j=1}^{n_{xi}} x_{ij} \] \[ \bar y_i = \frac{1}{n_{yi}} \Sigma_{j=1}^{n_{yi}} y_{ij} \] \[ \bar d_i = \bar x_i - \bar y_i \] \[ \bar d = \Sigma_{=1}^{n}\frac{d_i}{n} \] \[ s_{xi}^2 = \Sigma_{j=1}^{n_{xi}} \frac{(x_{xj}- \bar x_i)^2}{n_{xi}-1} \] \[ s_{yi}^2 = \Sigma_{j=1}^{n_{yi}} \frac{(y_{ij}- \bar y_i)^2}{n_{yi}-1} \] \[ s_{\bar d}^2 = \Sigma_{j=1}^{n} \frac{(d_{}- \bar d)^2}{n-1} \] Step 2: Compute pooled estimates within subject errors \[ s^2_{xw} = \Sigma_{=1}^{n} [\frac{n_{xi} -1}{N_x -1} \cdot s^2_{xi}] \] \[ s^2_{yw} = \Sigma_{=1}^{n} [\frac{n_{yi} -1}{N_y -1} \cdot s^2_{yi}] \] Step 3: Compute Harmonic Means Replicates \[ m_{xh} = \frac{n}{\Sigma_{=1}^n \frac{1}{n_{xi}}} \] \[ m_{yh} = \frac{n}{\Sigma_{=1}^n \frac{1}{n_{yi}}} \] Step 4: Compute variance differences \[ s^2_d = s^2_{\bar d} + (1+\frac{1}{m_{xh}}) \cdot s^2_{xw} + (1+\frac{1}{m_{yh}}) \cdot s^2_{yw} \] Step 5: Compute MOVER Components \[ S_{11} = s_{\bar d}^2 \cdot (1 - \frac{n-1}{\chi^2_{(1-\alpha, n-1)}}) \] \[ S_{12} = (1-\frac{1}{m_{xh}}) \cdot (1 - \frac{N_x-n}{\chi^2_{(1-\alpha, N_x-n)}}) \cdot s^2_{xw} \] \[ S_{13} = (1-\frac{1}{m_{yh}}) \cdot (1 - \frac{N_y-n}{\chi^2_{(1-\alpha, N_y-n)}}) \cdot s^2_{yw} \] \[ S_1 = \sqrt{S_{11}^2 +S_{12}^2 +S_{13}^2} \] \[ l = s_d^2 - S_1 \] \[ u = s_d^2 + S_1 \] \[ LME = \sqrt{\frac{z^2_{\alpha} \cdot s_d^2}{n} + z^2_{\beta/2} \cdot(\sqrt{u} - \sqrt{s^2_d})^2} \] \[ RME = \sqrt{\frac{z^2_{\alpha} \cdot s_d^2}{n} + z^2_{\beta/2} \cdot(\sqrt{l} - \sqrt{s^2_d})^2} \] ### LoA \[ LoA_{lower} = \bar d - z_{\beta/2} \cdot s_d \] \[ LoA_{upper} = \bar d + z_{\beta/2} \cdot s_d \]

title: Agreement for Categorical and Ordinal Ratings
text: Take example Gwet (2014): 12 subjects rated 4 raters 5-point scale, ratings missing. simplest summary percent agreement: proportion pairs ratings subject agree. agreement happen chance even raters guessed. chance-corrected coefficients take form \[ \frac{p_a - p_e}{1 - p_e}, \] \(p_a\) observed agreement \(p_e\) agreement expected chance: 1 means perfect agreement 0 means agreement chance. default coefficient Gwet’s AC1 (Gwet 2008). results cac_test() match irrCAC package (Gwet 2019).
code: ratings <- data.frame(   Rater1 = c(1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 1, 4, 1, 2, NA, NA, NA),   Rater2 = c(1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 2, 4, 1, 2, 5, NA, NA),   Rater3 = c(NA, 3, 3, 3, 2, 3, 4, 2, 2, 5, 1, 3),   Rater4 = c(1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 4, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, NA)) raters <- c("Rater1", "Rater2", "Rater3", "Rater4") cac_test(col.names = raters, data = ratings, coef = "pa") #>  #>  Percent agreement for 4 raters #>  #> data:  Rater1, Rater2, Rater3, Rater4 #>  #> alternative hypothesis: two.sided #> 95 percent confidence interval: #>  0.5417184 1.0000000 #> sample estimates: #> percent agreement  #>         0.8181818 cac_test(col.names = raters, data = ratings) #>  #>  Gwet's AC1 for 4 raters #>  #> data:  Rater1, Rater2, Rater3, Rater4 #>  #> alternative hypothesis: two.sided #> 95 percent confidence interval: #>  0.4608133 1.0000000 #> sample estimates: #> Gwet's AC1  #>  0.7754441

(2017) proposed model-based kappa, \(\kappa_m\), setting. fits ordinal (cumulative probit) mixed model rating subject \(\) rater \(j\) depends latent variable subject effect \(u_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2_u)\) rater effect \(v_j \sim N(0, \sigma^2_v)\): \[ P(Y_{ij} \le c \mid u_i, v_j) = \Phi(\alpha_c - u_i - v_j). \] \(\kappa_m\) chance-corrected probability two raters population put subject population category. depends number categories \(\rho = \sigma^2_u / (\sigma^2_u + \sigma^2_v + 1)\), share latent variance due real differences subjects. thresholds \(\alpha_c\) drop , \(\kappa_m\) affected common category , avoids kappa paradox . ord_kappa_test() requires ordinal package, fits model Laplace approximation. least 3 raters needed estimate rater variance, preferably many ; raters, use cac_test().

code: set.seed(2017) d <- expand.grid(id = 1:60, rater = paste0("R", 1:10)) latent <- rnorm(60, sd = 1.5)[d$id] + rnorm(10, sd = 0.5)[d$rater] +   rnorm(nrow(d)) d$rating <- cut(latent, c(-Inf, -1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5, Inf), labels = FALSE)  res_km <- ord_kappa_test(rating ~ rater | id, data = d) res_km #>  #>  Model-based kappa (ordinal probit GLMM) for 10 raters and 5 categories #>  #> data:  rating ~ rater | id #>  #> alternative hypothesis: two.sided #> 95 percent confidence interval: #>  0.2073107 0.3290732 #> sample estimates: #>   kappa_m  #> 0.2650766 res_km$fit[c("sigma2_subject", "sigma2_rater", "rho", "p0")] #> $sigma2_subject #> [1] 2.953053 #>  #> $sigma2_rater #> [1] 0.171657 #>  #> $rho #> [1] 0.715942 #>  #> $p0 #> [1] 0.4208256 cac_test(rating ~ rater | id, data = d, coef = "fleiss")$estimate #> Fleiss' kappa  #>      0.276016

text: experienced raters agree better inexperienced ones? raters agree better older patients’ scans? group, ord_kappa_test() fits model Nelson et al. (2017) group fixed effect separate rater (subject) variance group, compares groups. last five raters made variable. estimates \(\kappa_m\) group, interval difference, p-value likelihood ratio test equal rater variances two groups. fit$subgroups also gives \(\kappa_m\) rater group:  subject characteristic, patient age, use group_type = "subject"; group must constant within subject (, rater groups, within rater). Nelson et al. (2017) add random slope group indicator test variance correlation mixture chi-square distributions. group constant within rater (subject), intercept-slope covariance model identified, ord_kappa_test() fits equivalent model one variance per group, likelihood kappas, compares likelihood ratio statistic chi-square distribution 1 df. simulations equal variances (60 subjects, 16 raters), type error 0.044 0.05 level.
code: d$experience <- ifelse(d$rater %in% paste0("R", 1:5), "experienced",                        "novice") novice <- d$experience == "novice" d$rating2 <- cut(latent + novice * rnorm(10, sd = 1)[d$rater],                  c(-Inf, -1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5, Inf), labels = FALSE)  res_g <- ord_kappa_test(rating2 ~ rater | id, data = d,                         group = "experience") res_g #>  #>  Model-based kappa by rater group (experience): likelihood ratio test of #>  a group-specific rater variance #>  #> data:  rating2 ~ rater | id, rater group: experience #> LRT = 4.3937, p-value = 0.03607 #> alternative hypothesis: true difference in kappa_m is not equal to 0 #> 95 percent confidence interval: #>  -0.190612777 -0.003347343 #> sample estimates: #> kappa_m (experienced)      kappa_m (novice)  #>             0.2823913             0.1854113 res_g$fit$subgroups #>                subgroup   kappa_m         se     lower     upper #> 1           experienced 0.2823913 0.03379467 0.2210622 0.3530238 #> 2                novice 0.1854113 0.05032477 0.1059144 0.3042706 #> 3 experienced vs novice 0.2201790 0.04262563 0.1478964 0.3147403 summary(res_g) #> The likelihood ratio test is statistically significant (LRT = 4.39, p = #> 0.036) at the 0.05 alpha level: it can be stated that agreement differs #> between the rater groups (experience; null hypothesis: the rater #> variance is the same in both groups, so the group kappas are equal). In #> this model, kappa_m was 0.282 (95% CI [0.221, 0.353]) for raters in #> group experienced and 0.185 (95% CI [0.106, 0.304]) in group novice; #> the difference (novice minus experienced) was -0.0970 (95% CI [-0.191, #> -0.00335]). Between a rater from each group, kappa_m was 0.220. The #> model-based kappa (Nelson, Mitani & Edwards, 2017) was estimated from a #> cumulative probit mixed model with the group as a fixed effect and a #> separate rater variance in each group: a subject variance of 3.32 and #> rater variances of 0.165 and 1.43 in groups experienced and novice. The #> data had 60 subjects and 10 raters (600 ratings). The likelihood ratio #> test compares this model with one with a common rater variance #> (chi-square, 1 df); intervals use delta-method standard errors and are #> approximate. plot(res_g, type = "effects")

text: theoretically valid, still experimental, enhancement dem_reg pb_reg functions addition joint confidence regions slope intercept parameters. Traditional confidence intervals treat parameter separately, regression analysis, parameters correlated. Joint confidence regions account correlation creating elliptical region (intercept, slope) parameter space. approach, promoted Sadler (2010), provides several advantages: Higher Statistical Power: ellipse typically requires 20-50% fewer samples traditional confidence intervals detect bias Accounts Parameter Correlation: measurement range narrow, slope intercept highly negatively correlated Appropriate Test: Testing point (e.g., slope=1, intercept=0) naturally done region, separate intervals power advantage pronounced ratio maximum minimum X values small (< 10:1), common clinical method comparisons.

title: Errors-in-Variables Regression
text: Deming regression assumes paired measures (\(x_i, \space  y_i\)) measured error. \[ x_i = X_i + \epsilon_i \] \[ y_i = Y_i + \delta_i \] can measure relationship two variables following model. \[ \hat Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \hat X_i \] Traditionally 2 null hypotheses. First, intercept equal zero: \[ H_0: \beta_0 = 0 \space vs. \space H_1: \beta_0 \ne 0 \] Second, slope equal one: \[ H_0: \beta_1 = 1 \space vs. \space H_1: \beta_0 \ne 1 \]

title: Errors-in-Variables Regression
text: First, 3 components (\(v_x, \space v_y, \space cov_{xy}\)) \[ v_x = \Sigma_{=1}^N \space \hat w_i \cdot (x_i- \bar x_w)^2 \] \[ v_y = \Sigma_{=1}^N \space \hat w_i \cdot (y_i- \bar y_w)^2 \] \[ cov_{xy} = \Sigma_{=1}^N \space \hat w_i \cdot  (x_i- \bar x_w) \cdot (y_i- \bar y_w) \] slope (\(b_1\)) can estimated following equation. \[ b_1 = \frac{(\lambda \cdot v_y - v_x) + \sqrt{(v_x-\lambda \cdot v_y)^2 + 4 \cdot \lambda \cdot cov_{xy}^2}}{2 \cdot \lambda \cdot cov_{xy}} \] intercept (\(b_0\)) can estimated following equation. \[ b_0 = \bar y_w - b_1 \cdot \bar x_w \] standard errors b1 b0 estimated using jackknife method (detailed Linnet (1990)).

title: Reliability Analysis
text: Reliability studies ask two related questions. Relative reliability asks whether measurement ranks subjects consistently; summarised intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), proportion observed variance due real differences subjects. Absolute reliability asks much single measurement varies around subject’s true value; summarised standard error measurement (SEM), also called typical error (Hopkins 2000), often expressed coefficient variation. calculations follow Weir (2005), turn relies Shrout Fleiss (1979) McGraw Wong (1996). SimplyAgree one function question, returning standard htest object confidence interval , optionally, test: older reli_stats() reli_aov(), return everything , superseded (see Legacy functions). functions accept data three ways: formula, values ~ item | id; long data, measure, item id column names; wide data, one row per subject, item columns col.names. item whatever repeated: trial, occasion, rater, judge. example, take data Shrout Fleiss (1979) (6 subjects rated 4 judges).

title: Limits of Agreement — agreement_limit
text: x Name column first measurement y Name column measurement compare first. id Column subject identifier. Default "id" entry provided. data Data frame data. data_type type data structure. Options include "simple" (independent data points), "nest" (nested data) "reps" (replicated data points). loa_calc method limits agreement confidence intervals calculated. Options "mover" (Methods Recovering Variances method) "blandlatman" (Bland-Altman method). bound_type claim confidence bounds limits agreement (lower_loa_ci/upper_loa_ci) support. "iu" (default) gives one-sided 1 - alpha bound limit (outer ends 1 - 2 * alpha two-sided intervals). give intersection-union test, level alpha, whether limits agreement lie within maximal allowable difference, joint 1 - alpha interval limits. "joint" gives one-sided 1 - alpha/2 bound limit (outer ends 1 - alpha two-sided intervals, Bland-Altman convention), least 1 - alpha joint confidence limits. See details. agree.level agreement level required. Default 95%. proportion data lie thresholds, 95% limits agreement 0.95. alpha alpha-level confidence levels. prop_bias Logical indicator (TRUE/FALSE) whether proportional bias considered limits agreement calculations. Note non-zero slope differences average can appear without true proportional bias whenever two methods unequal measurement error variances, cov(difference, average) = (var(x) - var(y)) / 2 (Bland & Altman, 1999); errors--variables methods dem_reg() pb_reg() better suited assessing proportional bias. log_tf Calculate limits agreement using log-transformed data. log_tf_display type presentation log-transformed results. differences methods can displayed "ratio" "sympercent". lmer_df Degrees freedom method, matters data_type "nest". title: Limits of Agreement — agreement_limit
text: limits agreement (LoA) calculated function based method originally detailed Bland & Atlman (1986 & 1999). loa_calc allow users specify calculative method LoA can based Bland-Altman (1999) (loa_calc = "blandaltman"), accurate MOVER method Zou (2013) Donner & Zou (2012) (loa_calc = "mover"). confidence bounds limits agreement answer one two questions, set bound_type: "iu" (default): "Can conclude agreement within plus minus delta?" lower_loa_ci > -delta upper_loa_ci < delta, reject level alpha either limit agreement lies outside plus minus delta. conf.level (1 - alpha) applies side separately; bounds hold together 1 - 2 * alpha time. "joint": "limits agreement?" least 1 - alpha confidence, limits agreement lie lower_loa_ci upper_loa_ci. Used test plus minus delta, error rate alpha/2 (conservative). one-sided bound (1 - agree.level)/2 percentile one-sided tolerance bound, bounds equal-tailed tolerance bounds; target quantities tolerance_limit(bound_type = "iu"). bias confidence interval (lower.CL/upper.CL) always two-sided 1 - alpha interval.

The estimate is #> Fleiss' kappa: agreement corrected for chance agreement from the #> overall category proportions (observed agreement 0.975, chance #> agreement 0.818). Partial agreement between categories was credited #> with quadratic weights. The data had 12 subjects, of whom 1 had a #> single rating, rated by 4 raters (41 ratings) in 5 categories. Values in this interval are the most compatible with the data, #> given the model and its assumptions. The estimate is the two-way, #> consistency, single-measure ICC (McGraw & Wong ICC(C,1); Shrout & #> Fleiss ICC(3,1)): the reliability of a single measurement, excluding #> systematic differences between items. code: # Weir (2005) data set A: 8 subjects, 2 trials weir <- data.frame(t1 = c(146, 148, 170, 90, 157, 156, 176, 205),                    t2 = c(140, 152, 152, 99, 145, 153, 167, 218)) mdc_test(col.names = c("t1", "t2"), data = weir) #>  #> 	Minimal detectable change (95%, two-sided) from the standard error of #> 	measurement (two-way, consistency) #>  #> data:  t1, t2 #>  #> alternative hypothesis: two.sided #> 95 percent confidence interval: #>  13.84918 42.63152 #> sample estimates: #>      MDC  #> 20.94635  #>   # Can a change of 30 units be distinguished from measurement error? res <- mdc_test(col.names = c("t1", "t2"), data = weir, null.value = 30) summary(res) #> The test is not statistically significant (X-squared(7) = 3.41, p = #> 0.156; MDC = 20.9, 95% upper bound 37.6) at the 0.05 alpha level. The #> null hypothesis cannot be rejected: at the desired error rate, it #> cannot be stated that the true MDC is less than 30. The estimate is the #> minimal detectable change (two-way, consistency), in the units of the #> measurement, from the SEM excluding systematic differences between #> items: the smallest change in either direction between two measurements #> of one subject that exceeds measurement error with 95% confidence, 1.96 #> * sqrt(2) * SEM. It applies to an individual's change, not to an #> average (group) effect, which should be judged by its own confidence #> interval. The data had 8 subjects and 2 items (16 measurements, none #> missing); variance components were estimated by analysis of variance. #> The interval and chi-square test are exact under normality (chi-square #> distribution of the error variance).  # From an existing SEM, one-sided, as a percentage (log scale) # in the result we can access the MDC on the percentage scale (converted from sympercent) sem <- reli_err_test(col.names = c("t1", "t2"), data = weir, scale = "log") res_log <- mdc_test(sem, sided = "one.sided") res_log$percent #>     change estimate    lower    upper #> 1 increase 12.42008 8.047983 26.90570 #> 2 decrease 11.04792 7.448527 21.20134

title: SimplyAgree 0.4.0
text: New icc_test(): one intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), chosen model, type unit (McGraw & Wong forms, Shrout & Fleiss names), returned htest. Two-sided F-based intervals, optional F test null.value (default NULL: estimate interval , since testing ICC 0 rarely informative), method = "reml" missing data (observed-data degrees freedom, warning), optional subject bootstrap (boot = TRUE) whose interval type standard error chosen simulations. New reli_err_test(): standard error measurement (SEM), estimate (SEE) prediction (SEP), intervals optional test acceptable error. scale = "log" (sympercents) scale = "mean" give coefficients variation. New mdc_test(): minimal detectable change (MDC, also SDD/SRD repeatability coefficient), 1.96 × √2 × SEM default, interval (SEM interval, scaled) optional test change matters. works data existing reli_err_test() SEM, offers one-sided MDCs (sided), scores averaged several trials (k_avg), percentage increases decreases log scale. documentation explains MDC individual threshold (group effects counting “responders”) “smallest worthwhile change” computed reliability data. New power_icc() precision_icc(): power sample size ICC F test, sample size ICC confidence interval given width given assurance (exact F-based calculations one-way consistency ICCs, single average measures (unit), plus Walter et al. Zou approximations). missing, expected proportion missing measurements, give approximate calculation REML analysis incomplete data, checked simulation 30% missing. documentation explains use guide agreement ICCs (optimistic lower bound sample size), missing data non-normal data. New summary(), plot() check() methods results. summary(style = "estimation") describes interval compatibility interval converts p-value S-value; style = "hypothesis" gives usual test decision. plot() shows subjects across items item means 95% CIs, , type, subjects ordered mean ("subjects"), deviations subject mean item ("items"), pair items line identity ("pairs"). check() adds additivity panel Mandel’s test non-additivity (items differ scale; built fitted additive model Milliken & Graybill, also works missing measurements) within-subject SD subject mean, show whether error grows mean. ICC confidence intervals now two-sided. previously used conf.level tail (qf(1 - alpha)), “95%” interval really 90% interval (limit one-sided 95% bound). intervals now match Shrout & Fleiss (1979), McGraw & Wong (1996), psych, irr, SPSS Stata. reproduce old numbers conf.level = c, use conf.level = 1 - 2 * (1 - c) (e.g. old 0.95 = new 0.90). one-sided lower bound ICC, use icc_test(alternative = "greater"). reli_stats() missing data now uses degrees freedom based observed data (warns intervals approximate), instead complete-data degrees freedom. reli_aov() now drops every subject measured every item (including subjects missing row long data, previously analysed wrong degrees freedom), message. variance components reli_aov() now use ANOVA estimates (item variance previously MSW - MSE). other_ci = TRUE type = "chisq", intervals SEE, SEP, ICC-based SEM CV now use delta method (log scale); chi-square interval error degrees freedom Vangel’s CV interval apply statistics. SEM error mean square keeps exact chi-square interval. bootstrap intervals (type = "perc", "norm" "basic") now resample subjects functions (reli_stats() previously used parametric bootstrap). cv_calc = "residuals" (downward-biased version "MSE") replaced "MSE" warning. print() longer fails conf.level other_ci passed variable. Long data one measurement per subject item now error (aggregate first). jamovi reliability analysis now uses icc_test() reli_err_test(): two-sided ICC intervals, intervals SEM, SEE SEP (SEE SEP now use SD matched ICC’s denominator), CV sympercents, REML measurements missing. power sample size vignette new section planning reliability studies power_icc() precision_icc() (tests interval widths, trading subjects trials, average measures, missing measurements, using calculations guide agreement ICCs).

title: SimplyAgree 0.4.0
text: New cac_test(): one chance-corrected agreement coefficient categorical ratings (Gwet’s AC1/AC2, Fleiss’ kappa, Krippendorff’s alpha, percent agreement), returned htest optional t test null.value. takes formula, long wide interfaces icc_test(), accepts numeric, character factor ratings, offers Gwet’s weighting schemes ("quadratic", "linear", "ordinal", "radical", "ratio", "circular", "bipolar") custom weight matrix. Results match irrCAC package. New ord_kappa_test(): model-based kappa Nelson & Edwards (2015) Nelson, Mitani & Edwards (2017) ordinal ratings many raters (#63). computed cumulative probit mixed model crossed subject rater random effects (fitted ordinal::clmm(); ordinal now Suggests), affected category prevalence, returns rater effects (conditional modes). interval formed logit subject variance share, stays within [0, 1]. group, compares two groups raters (e.g. experienced inexperienced) subjects (e.g. younger older patients): group fixed effect rater (subject) variance, result gives kappa_m group, interval difference, kappa rater group, likelihood ratio test equal variances. model identified form random-slope model Nelson et al. (2017), whose intercept-slope covariance identified group constant within raters subjects. New summary() plot() methods : category use rater, ratings subject, (ord_kappa_test()) rater effects. New vignette, “Agreement Categorical Ordinal Ratings”, covering choose coefficient (including kappa paradox), weights ordinal scales, rating scale, model-based kappa, rater effects, group comparisons. inter-rater section reliability vignette now points . longer fails ratings one category (chance-corrected coefficients returned NA, warning). New categories argument scale points never used. Gwet’s AC1/AC2 weights depend full set categories, wrong category unused. New weights argument weighting schemes (weighted = TRUE still means quadratic weights). Long data one rating per subject rater now error; extra ratings silently dropped. Lower confidence limits clipped possible range coefficient (clipped 1). row name “Kririppendorff’s Alpha” now “Krippendorff’s Alpha”.
